messages.author: 410e477af3aeaf0d
messages.subject: Identifying False Positives by Shape
parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to plot some tabular data I've got in a similar fashion to
an example in Tufte's "The Visual Display of Quantative Information".
The particular image I'm trying to emulate is Consumer Review car
maintenance plot on page 174.

I've got two files of relationship information for an experiment I'm
running. The first file contains the relations which exist. The second
file is the relationships uncovered by some code I've written. What I
want to achieve is a plot with circles where a relationship does exist
and is detected, with the amount of fill in the circle being the
proportion of runs where this relationship was detected.

The problem I'm having is I also want to highlight the false positives
where a relationship has been detected which isn't part of the answer.
I want to plot this as a different shape to make it clear.

My example file is:
A E
A F
B H
B I

And the detections are:
A E
A E
A F
B H
B I
B H
B I
A I

#So far I'm reading the files in:
example <- read.table("example.txt")
detections <- read.table("detections.txt")

#and plotting the expected values as circles:
p <- ggplot(example, aes(V1, V2)) + geom_point(size = 10)

# Calculate the Frequencies of the detections and subset to include
only those which were found
detections.frame <- as.data.frame.table(table(detections))
detections.frame <- subset(detections.frame, Freq > 0)

# Now I add the points which were detected as circles whose size
depends on the number of times they were found.
p <- p + geom_point(aes(Var1, Var2, size = 1/Freq), data =
detections.frame, colour = "grey90")

I don't know how to identify the incorrect detections and then plot
them as a different shape. Does anyone have any suggestions?

Thanks
Alastair

messages.author: b26ea422f70d3a1f
messages.subject: Re: Identifying False Positives by Shape
parts:
If I understand your problem, I believe you can identify your incorrect items with something like:

> incorrect <- (table (detections) * (1 - table (example)))
> incorrect.frame <- subset (as.data.frame (incorrect), Freq > 0)

Though perhaps there are nice set operators in R that I don't generally use.* And my little "1-table..." thing assumes there is only one example of each combination, which is a bit sloppy.

Similarly, you can get a correct.frame, then rbind the two together with an additional factor indicating which are the correct and which are the incorrect, so you can use that in ggplot2 to determine the color/shape, etc.

* A quick look shows me that this kind of set-based thing works, somewhat:

> a <- vector (mode="list")
> a[[1]] <- c("A", "B")
> a[[2]] <- c("C", "D")
> b <- vector (mode="list")
> b[[1]] <- c("A", "B")
> b[[2]] <- c("G", "H")
> union (a, b)
[[1]]
[1] "A" "B"

[[2]]
[1] "C" "D"

[[3]]
[1] "G" "H"

> intersect (a, b)
[[1]]
[1] "A" "B"

> setdiff (a, intersect (a, b))
[[1]]
[1] "C" "D"

But then table no longer works as you'd like without some kind of fancy conversion.

messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: Identifying False Positives by Shape
parts:
Hi Alaistair,

I'd try something like this:

example$correct <- TRUE

detections <- merge(detections, example, all.x = T, by = c("V1", "V2"))
detections$correct[is.na(detections$correct)] <- FALSE

counts <- as.data.frame(with(detections, table(V1, V2, correct))
qplot(V1, V2, data = counts, size = Freq, shape = correct)

Hadley
